title: The Exit Is a Second Loan You Do Not Yet Have
summary: A construction loan is repaid by something outside it: a sale or a permanent loan sized to the finished building. The exit cap rate sets the size of that next loan, and the maturity gap measures whether the building can earn its refinance before the construction loan falls due.
body:
A construction loan is borrowed against its own exit. Before the first shovel goes in, you must know who will repay it, on what numbers and by what date, because the building does not choose its exit; the market does.

Recall

Q. What is a cash trap in a loan agreement?

A. A covenant level, set above the default level, at which surplus cash stops flowing to the borrower and is held in a lender-controlled account until the test is met again. The levels are commercial practice, negotiated loan by loan.

Q. Name three country risks beyond ordinary market risk.

A. Currency mismatch, where you borrow in one currency and earn in another; convertibility, where you cannot exchange local currency; and transfer or expropriation risk, where you cannot move money out or the state takes the asset.

Q. In the capital stack, who is paid first?

A. Senior debt, then mezzanine debt, then preferred equity, then common equity. The lower a layer sits, the more it is paid for the risk it carries.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer can do everything right on site and still lose the building on a calendar date. The construction loan has a maturity date: the day the whole balance is due. Nothing in the loan pays it. Something outside the loan must: a sale, or a new and larger loan from a different lender. That outside event is called the exit, and on the day you sign the construction loan you do not yet have it. This week Priya and I teach you to treat the exit as a second financing you are already responsible for. I am Nadia; I read the accounts, and in the accounts the exit shows up long before it shows up on site.

The exit is a loan you do not yet have

In plain English: the construction lender expects to be repaid by someone else, so you need to know today what that someone else will want to see tomorrow.

The professional framing is take-out financing: the permanent loan, or sale proceeds, that repays the construction loan once the building is complete and earning. A permanent lender sizes its loan to the stabilised building, which means the building at its normal level of occupancy and income. It runs the same tests you learned in Week 36: loan to value, debt service coverage and debt yield. Every one of those tests depends on value or income at the time of the refinance, not at the time you started.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 30,000,000 dollar apartment project is funded with 10,000,000 dollars of equity and a 20,000,000 dollar construction loan. At stabilisation, net operating income (NOI), the income left after operating expenses and before debt service, is forecast at 2,000,000 dollars a year. If buyers and appraisers price the building at a 6 percent capitalisation rate, value is 2,000,000 divided by 0.06, about 33,330,000 dollars. A permanent lender willing to lend 65 percent of value, a commercial term rather than a standard, offers about 21,670,000 dollars. That repays the 20,000,000 dollars and leaves room for closing costs. The exit works.

The exit cap rate is the size of your next loan

In plain English: the rate used to turn income into value at the end decides how much the next lender will lend.

The professional framing is the exit capitalisation rate, often shortened to exit cap rate: the cap rate assumed when the stabilised building is valued for sale or refinance. It is usually set higher than today's going-in rate, because the future is uncertain and buildings age.

A second worked example. Same building, same 2,000,000 dollars of NOI, but rates have risen during construction and buildings now trade at 7 percent. Value is 2,000,000 divided by 0.07, about 28,570,000 dollars. At 65 percent, the permanent loan is about 18,570,000 dollars. The construction loan is 20,000,000 dollars. There is a shortfall of about 1,430,000 dollars before any closing costs. Nothing on site went wrong. The income is exactly as forecast. A one-point move in the cap rate turned a clean exit into a cash call on you.

Say that out loud now.

The exit cap rate is not a valuation detail. It is the size of my next loan.

The maturity gap

In plain English: the date the loan is due may come before the date the building can earn its own refinance.

The professional framing is the maturity gap: the time between the construction loan's maturity and the earliest date a take-out can realistically close. A hypothetical example: a 36-month construction loan; construction takes 24 months; lease-up, the period of filling the building with tenants, takes 15 months, so the building stabilises in month 39. Many permanent lenders, as commercial practice, want several months of actual income at the stabilised level before they will close, so the earliest refinance is around month 42. The gap is six months. On day one, the plan already does not reach its own exit.

There are three ways to close a gap, and each costs something. An extension option in the construction loan, which usually carries a fee and conditions. A bridge loan: short, expensive debt that repays the construction loan and buys time until stabilisation. Or a sale, which depends on a buyer market you do not control. A bridge buys time; it does not buy income. If the reason for the gap is weak demand, a bridge simply moves the problem to a more expensive lender.

My accountant's note. In many accounting frameworks, debt due within twelve months of the balance sheet date is presented as a current liability, and an auditor then asks whether the entity can meet its obligations as they fall due. Verify that against the applicable accounting standard before you rely on it. The practical effect is real: a loan that is fine in month 20 looks alarming in the financial statements by month 25, and your other lenders read those statements.

How the best do it

Disciplined institutional owners decide the exit before they commit to the build. Some arrange a forward commitment, a permanent lender's agreement in advance to fund on completion if defined conditions are met. Others simply underwrite the take-out at a stressed exit cap rate and a higher interest rate than today's, and choose a construction loan whose term plus extensions reaches well past the realistic stabilisation date. A small developer can copy the habit with one page, an exit card: the maturity date, the expected stabilisation date, the take-out loan sized at today's cap rate and at one point worse, the gap in dollars and months, and how each gap will be funded.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: refinance proceeds are generally borrowed money rather than income, but fees, prepayment costs and any distribution of excess proceeds may have tax consequences; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a completion or carry guarantee on the construction loan may stay alive until the take-out closes, so a late exit extends your personal exposure. Banking: the permanent lender will read the construction history, so clean reporting now is a cheaper refinance later. Governance: the decision to extend, bridge or sell should be authorised in writing before the deadline, not improvised at it. Estate: any guarantee that survives into a bridge must be known to your estate plan. Exit: the exit is the subject; write it down on the day you sign the construction loan.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, as borrower's counsel on maturity and extension terms; accredited appraiser, on stabilised value.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming the take-out will be there because the building will be good. A good building at the wrong cap rate, or at a stabilisation date after maturity, still fails. The control is to size the take-out at a stressed exit cap rate and to make the construction loan's term, with extensions, reach past the realistic stabilisation date with room to spare.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner models the exit at today's cap rate and today's interest rate, as if the market will wait. Then he picks the construction loan with the lowest margin and the shortest term, saving a little interest and buying a maturity gap he never priced.

Callback

In Week 10, Sage taught that value is income divided by a rate. That one line decides this whole week. In Week 36, Priya added that a loan is sized by its tightest test. Put them together: at the exit, the tightest test is usually loan to value, and loan to value moves with the cap rate. A small change in the denominator becomes a large change in the cash you must find.

Recap

The construction loan is repaid by an exit you do not yet have: a permanent loan or a sale. The permanent lender sizes to stabilised value, so the exit cap rate sets the size of the next loan. The maturity gap is the time between the loan's due date and the earliest realistic take-out, and it must be closed by extension, bridge or sale, each at a cost.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of a take-out that never arrived.
checklist: I have written down how the construction loan will be repaid, and by when.
I have sized the take-out loan at today's cap rate and at one point worse.
I know the realistic stabilisation date, including the months of income a permanent lender will want.
I have measured the maturity gap in months and in dollars.
I know the term, extension options, fees and conditions of the construction loan.
I have a funded plan for each gap: extension, bridge or sale.
I know which guarantees stay alive until the take-out closes.
I keep a one-page exit card and update it every quarter.
head: Field checklist
speak: A construction loan is repaid by something outside it. When the building is finished and earning, a permanent lender, or a buyer, takes out the construction lender. That take-out is a second financing, and on the day I sign the construction loan I do not have it yet. The permanent lender sizes to stabilised value, which is net operating income divided by the exit cap rate. So the exit cap rate is not a valuation detail; it is the size of my next loan. On 2,000,000 dollars of income, a move from 6 to 7 percent cuts the loan at 65 percent of value from about 21,670,000 to about 18,570,000 dollars, a shortfall against a 20,000,000 dollar construction loan. The maturity gap is the time between the loan's due date and the earliest realistic refinance. I close it in advance with an extension, a bridge or a sale, and I price each one before I start.
terms: Take-out financing — the permanent loan or sale proceeds that repay the construction loan once the building is complete and earning.
Exit cap rate — the capitalisation rate assumed when the stabilised building is valued for sale or refinance, usually set above today's rate.
Maturity gap — the time between the construction loan's maturity and the earliest date a take-out can realistically close.

hostile.q: Your construction loan matures in 36 months and your own schedule says you stabilise in month 39. Why should I lend to a plan that misses its own exit?
hostile.a: You should not, as drawn, and I am not asking you to. I have asked for two six-month extension options with defined conditions, and I am pricing a bridge as the fallback. I have also sized the take-out at a cap rate one point above today's, and the equity plan covers that shortfall. If you would rather match term to the schedule at a slightly higher margin, I will take that trade.

title: The Take-Out That Never Arrived: A Composite
summary: A composite case: an apartment building finished nearly on time and on budget was lost because its construction loan matured into a market that would not refinance it. The seven steps show a term shorter than the project's own path to stabilisation and an exit sized at the going-in cap rate.
body:
This is a composite example: a well-built apartment building that was finished on time and on budget, and still passed to its lender, because its construction loan fell due into a market that would not refinance it. The failure was in the calendar, not on site.

Recall

Q. What is a break-even in a stress test?

A. The value of one input, such as rent, vacancy or interest rate, at which the project just fails a stated test, with every other input held constant. It tells you how much room you have, in plain units.

Q. What happened to contracts in Argentina in 2002?

A. When the currency peg ended, the state converted many dollar contracts and deposits into pesos by law, so the terms people had relied on were changed by the government itself.

Q. What did the Stuyvesant Town case teach about the capital stack?

A. A stack built on a business plan rather than on existing income fails when the plan fails, because every layer above the equity was priced as if the plan had already succeeded.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Ford here, with Roman. Most of the failures we have studied were visible on site: a change nobody checked, a contractor who ran out of cash. This one is quieter. Nothing was built badly. A date arrived, and the money that was meant to meet it was not there. This is a composite example, assembled from a common pattern; the figures are hypothetical round numbers and no real project or firm is described.

1. Timeline

Year 0: a developer buys land and arranges a 24,000,000 dollar construction loan for a 36,000,000 dollar apartment building, with 12,000,000 dollars of equity. The loan is floating rate, interest only, with a 30-month term and one six-month extension option. Month 22: construction finishes, two months late. Month 26: lease-up is slower than planned; occupancy is 70 percent. Month 28: interest rates have risen sharply over the build, and cap rates for similar buildings have widened from about 5.5 to about 7 percent. Month 30: the developer exercises the extension and pays the fee. Month 33: the permanent lender's appraisal comes in well below plan. Month 36: maturity. The loan is not repaid. Month 41: after a forbearance period, the lender takes the building.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions set the course. Choosing a 30-month term to save margin, when the developer's own schedule showed stabilisation around month 34. Accepting only one extension, with a coverage test as its condition. And leaving the interest rate unhedged because the hedge was expensive at closing.

3. Assumptions

The model assumed the exit cap rate would equal the going-in rate, that lease-up would run at the pace of the strongest recent competitor, and that a permanent lender would lend 70 percent of value. Each was a single optimistic number, not a range, and all three were needed together for the exit to work.

4. Incentives

The developer's fee was earned at completion, so the team was rewarded for finishing the building, not for refinancing it. The construction lender priced the loan to its own risk and term, and was not asked to fund past maturity. The broker who placed the loan was paid on closing. Nobody in the transaction was paid to own the exit.

5. Warning signs ignored

Rates rose during construction, and every rise was visible on the monthly interest statement. Comparable buildings sold at widening cap rates and were reported in the market. The leasing team's weekly report showed tours converting more slowly than plan from month 24. Any one of these should have triggered an early refinance conversation, a year before maturity rather than at it.

Say that out loud now.

The exit is a date, and the market meets the date, not the plan.

6. Point of no return

Roman's view is that the point of no return was month 30, when the developer paid to extend without a funded plan for the gap. At that moment there were still options: sell at a reduced price, bring in rescue equity, or negotiate a longer extension while the lender still had choices too. Paying the fee spent cash and time and changed nothing about the arithmetic.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a construction loan whose term was shorter than the project's own realistic path to a refinance, combined with an exit sized at the going-in cap rate. The developer financed the building and assumed the exit.

The arithmetic at maturity

The numbers make the point. At month 33, the building's actual NOI, at 88 percent occupancy, is about 1,750,000 dollars a year. The appraiser uses a 7 percent cap rate: value is 1,750,000 divided by 0.07, about 25,000,000 dollars. The permanent lender offers 65 percent of value, about 16,250,000 dollars, and its coverage test on a higher rate gives less still. The construction loan, plus capitalised interest and the extension fee, stands at about 24,600,000 dollars. The gap is roughly 8,350,000 dollars, against an equity cheque that was 12,000,000 dollars on day one.

Now the same project with three controls. A 42-month term, which costs perhaps a quarter point more margin. An interest rate cap bought at closing. And an exit sized at 6.5 percent, one point above the going-in rate, with the equity plan covering the difference. At month 33 the developer is not yet at maturity, the capped rate keeps interest within the reserve, and there are nine months to reach stabilisation and sign a take-out. The loss of value from the cap rate move is real; it is now a lower profit, not a lost building.

What the lender saw

Roman adds the lender's view. At maturity, a construction lender does not want a building; it wants repayment. Its choices are to extend, to sell the loan, or to enforce. It extends when it believes the gap will close with time and the borrower has shown it can fund the carry. It enforces when the borrower has no plan and no cash. The developer who arrives at month 30 with a written plan and a deposit is negotiating; the one who arrives with a request is not.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating maturity as a formality that will be handled when it arrives. The control is to set a refinance start date, at least twelve months before maturity, and a written decision at that date: refinance, extend, sell or recapitalise.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner pays an extension fee to buy time without asking what the time is for. Time helps only if the cause of the gap is time. If the cause is value, more time costs more interest.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught that the severe case arrives as a combination. Here it did: a late finish, a slow lease-up, higher rates and a wider cap rate, each survivable alone, together fatal at one date. A stress test that had run those four together against the maturity date, rather than against stabilised value alone, would have shown the problem at closing.

The prevention rule

Rule 45: Never let a construction loan mature before the building can carry its own refinance at a stressed exit cap rate; match the term and extensions to the realistic stabilisation date, and fund the gap before I start.

Recap

A good building was lost to a calendar date. The term was too short, the exit was sized at the going-in cap rate, the rate was unhedged and nobody was paid to own the exit. The fix was cheap at closing and impossible at maturity.

Next: Priya, on The Money: what extensions, bridges and refinance gaps really cost.
checklist: My construction loan's term plus extensions reaches past my realistic stabilisation date.
I have sized the exit at a cap rate at least one point above the going-in rate.
I have decided whether to hedge the interest rate, in writing, with the cost stated.
I have a refinance start date at least twelve months before maturity.
I know the conditions for each extension option and test them every quarter.
I know who on my team is responsible for the exit, and how they are rewarded.
I will not pay an extension fee without a funded plan for the gap.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite example. A developer finished an apartment building close to on time and on budget, and still lost it, because the construction loan matured into a market that would not refinance it. The term was 30 months when the developer's own schedule showed stabilisation around month 34. The exit was sized at the going-in cap rate. Rates were left unhedged. While the building was being built, rates rose and cap rates widened from about 5.5 to about 7 percent. At maturity the permanent loan on offer was about 16,000,000 dollars against a balance of about 24,600,000. The point of no return was paying an extension fee without a funded plan. The root cause: financing the building and assuming the exit. Rule 45: never let a construction loan mature before the building can carry its own refinance at a stressed exit cap rate, and fund the gap before you start.
terms: Forbearance — a lender's agreement, for a defined period and on conditions, not to enforce a default it is entitled to enforce.
Extension option — a borrower's right, written into the loan, to extend maturity on stated conditions such as a fee and a coverage test.
Refinance start date — the date, set well before maturity, by which the exit must be decided and in progress.

hostile.q: You built the building well. Why did you not see the maturity coming?
hostile.a: We saw the date; we did not price it. The term was chosen to save margin and the exit was modelled at the going-in cap rate. The warning signs, rising rates, widening cap rates and slower leasing, were all in our own reports. My rule now is a refinance start date twelve months before maturity, an exit sized one point above the going-in cap rate, and a term that reaches past the realistic stabilisation date.

rule: Rule 45: Never let a construction loan mature before the building can carry its own refinance at a stressed exit cap rate; match the term and extensions to the realistic stabilisation date, and fund the gap before I start.

title: What a Late Exit Costs: Carry, Fees, Rate and Proceeds
summary: A late exit costs more than interest: extension fees, a pricier bridge loan and a smaller refinance all come out of a thin layer of equity. This lesson prices each cost, shows why a bridge only works when time is the cause of the gap, and compares the late case with the small cost of preventing it.
body:
An exit that arrives late does not just cost interest. It costs fees, a higher rate, a smaller loan and time, and because your profit is a thin layer on top of a large cost, every one of those lands on your return at a multiple.

Recall

Q. When presenting stress tests to a committee, what comes after the nearest threshold?

A. The combination that gets you there, then the priced actions: what each protection costs and what it changes in the severe case.

Q. Name the three ways currency risk hits a project.

A. It raises debt service in local terms, it reduces the value of income in the lender's currency, and it can break coverage covenants, so it affects coverage, value and return at once.

Q. Why does mezzanine debt cost more than senior debt?

A. Because it sits below the senior loan and is repaid only after it, so it absorbs losses first and is priced for that risk.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Priya here. Yesterday Ford showed a building lost to a date. Today we price the date. Most developers can tell you their construction interest rate. Few can tell you what three extra months before refinance do to their internal rate of return, the annual return that makes the present value of all the cash flows equal to zero. That is the number your investors care about, and it moves more than you expect.

The four costs of a late exit

In plain English: when the exit slips, you pay more for the money you already have, and you get less of the money you were counting on.

The professional framing names four costs. First, carry: interest on a loan that is almost fully drawn, running for longer. Second, fees: extension fees, typically a fraction of a percent of the loan, and the costs of any new lender, as commercial practice. Third, rate: a bridge loan is priced above a construction loan, because it is short and is used when other lenders have said no. Fourth, proceeds: a refinance done in a weaker market, or before stabilisation, is smaller, so more of your equity stays trapped.

A worked example, hypothetical. A 30,000,000 dollar project, 20,000,000 dollar construction loan at 8 percent, fully drawn at completion. The planned exit is month 30. It slips six months. Carry: 20,000,000 times 8 percent times half a year, 800,000 dollars. Extension fee at 0.5 percent: 100,000 dollars. Total: 900,000 dollars, all coming out of profit, because the building's value has not changed.

The bridge: buying time at a price

In plain English: a bridge loan is a short loan that repays the construction lender so you can wait for the building to stabilise.

The professional framing is bridge financing: short-term debt, usually one to three years, priced higher and often with more fees, secured on a building that is not yet stabilised. It is the right tool when the cause of the gap is time: a building that will earn its permanent loan once it is full. It is the wrong tool when the cause is value: a building that will not support the permanent loan even when full.

A second worked example. The construction loan of 20,000,000 dollars matures. A bridge lender offers 20,000,000 dollars at 10 percent for 12 months, with a 1 percent fee at entry and a 0.5 percent fee at exit. Cost for the year: interest 2,000,000 dollars, fees 300,000 dollars, total 2,300,000 dollars. Against that, NOI during the year as the building fills is perhaps 1,200,000 dollars. The bridge's net cost is about 1,100,000 dollars. Worth it if, at the end, the stabilised building refinances for enough to repay the bridge. Not worth it if it does not, because then you have paid 1,100,000 dollars to arrive at the same gap a year later.

Say that out loud now.

A bridge buys time, not income. I use it only when time is the cause of the gap.

What it does to the return

Take the hypothetical project: 30,000,000 dollars of cost, 10,000,000 dollars of equity, and a plan to refinance at month 30 on stabilised NOI of 2,000,000 dollars at a 6 percent cap rate. Value is about 33,330,000 dollars, so the profit on paper is about 3,330,000 dollars, a third of the equity. A permanent loan at 65 percent of value, about 21,670,000 dollars, repays the 20,000,000 dollar construction loan and leaves a little over for costs.

Now the late case. Six months of slip cost 900,000 dollars. The cap rate is half a point wider, 6.5 percent, so value is 2,000,000 divided by 0.065, about 30,770,000 dollars, a fall of about 2,560,000 dollars. Profit on paper falls from about 3,330,000 dollars to a small loss of about 130,000 dollars. And the refinance at 65 percent is now about 20,000,000 dollars, which only just repays the original loan and nothing of the extra carry, so you write a cheque at maturity. Six months and half a point erased the whole profit.

The equity multiple, total cash returned divided by equity invested, measures size; the internal rate of return measures size and time together, and a late exit takes away both. The lesson is leverage on the downside. Your 10,000,000 dollars is a thin layer on top of a 30,000,000 dollar cost. Every dollar of extra cost and every dollar of lost value comes out of that layer first.

What a prepaid exit costs, and why it is cheap

The controls are not free. A longer construction term, say 42 months instead of 30, might cost a quarter point more margin: on an average balance of about 12,000,000 dollars over the build, perhaps 30,000 dollars a year, about 100,000 dollars across the term. An interest rate cap might cost a few hundred thousand dollars at closing. A larger equity cheque, sized to the stressed exit, lowers your internal rate of return in the base case. Put the controls side by side with the swing of about 3,460,000 dollars in the late case, and they are cheap. That is the trade: pay a known small amount now so that the late case is a disappointment rather than a cash call.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. An exit you have not yet secured is a contingent liability: a possible future demand for cash. If you have guaranteed carry or completion, a late exit can move that demand from the project to you. On your own sheet, list each project's maturity date, the stressed refinance gap and the guarantees that cover it, and make sure your liquidity floor, the cash you never spend, could meet the largest single gap without selling something else in a hurry. Professional sign-off required: a licensed financial adviser before you act on any of this.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is measuring a late exit in interest alone. The interest is the smallest of the four costs; the lost proceeds are usually the largest. The control is to model the late case in full: carry, fees, rate and proceeds, run to internal rate of return as well as to profit.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner takes a bridge loan at maturity because it is available, without first proving that the stabilised building will repay it. A bridge without a proven take-out is a more expensive way to default later.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage warned that the internal rate of return can mislead because it rewards speed and ignores size. Today the warning runs the other way: a late exit hurts the internal rate of return more than the multiple, because it takes away time. Report both to your investors, and explain why they moved differently.

Recap

A late exit costs carry, fees, rate and proceeds, and the lost proceeds are usually largest. A bridge is right only when the gap is caused by time. Because equity is a thin layer, small exit costs cut the return hard. The controls, longer term, a hedge and equity sized to the stressed exit, are cheap beside the late case.

Next: LEX, on The Rules: maturity, extension options and take-out commitments, and how that paper is read.
checklist: I have modelled a late exit with all four costs: carry, fees, rate and proceeds.
I report both the internal rate of return and the equity multiple for the late case.
I know what a bridge loan would cost in interest and fees for one year.
I use a bridge only when I can prove the stabilised building repays it.
I have priced a longer term and a rate hedge against the late case.
My personal balance sheet lists each maturity and the guarantees behind it.
My liquidity floor could meet the largest single refinance gap.
head: Field checklist
speak: A late exit costs four things. Carry: interest running longer on an almost fully drawn loan. Fees: extension fees and a new lender's costs. Rate: a bridge loan is priced above the construction loan. And proceeds: a refinance in a weaker market is smaller. On a hypothetical 20,000,000 dollar loan at 8 percent, six months of slip costs about 800,000 dollars of interest plus fees. A half-point wider cap rate cuts proceeds by more than that. Because my equity is a thin layer on top of the total cost, these costs can cut the profit by a third, and the internal rate of return by more, because time is what a late exit takes away. A bridge buys time, not income, so I use it only when time is the cause of the gap. The cures, a longer term, a hedge and equity sized to the stressed exit, are cheap beside the late case.
terms: Bridge financing — short-term, higher-priced debt that repays a construction loan and buys time until the building stabilises.
Carry — the cost of holding a project over time, chiefly interest on borrowed money, plus taxes and insurance.
Contingent liability — a possible future obligation that becomes real only if a defined event happens, such as a guarantee being called.

hostile.q: You want a bridge loan at 10 percent. What makes you sure the permanent lender will repay me in a year?
hostile.a: I am not asking you to rely on hope. Here is the leasing evidence: signed leases and the rate of conversion over the last three months. Here is the take-out sized at stabilised income and a cap rate half a point above the latest comparable sales, and it repays your loan with room to spare. If occupancy is below the agreed level at month 9, I will either inject equity or start a sale, and I will accept that as a written covenant.

title: Maturity, Extensions and the Take-Out Commitment: How the Paper Is Read
summary: At maturity, three pieces of paper decide what happens: the extension option, any take-out commitment and the default and enforcement terms. This lesson reads each one, shows why an extension test set to the base case fails in the downside, and compares how Canada and Guyana approach mortgage enforcement.
body:
At maturity the loan agreement stops being about construction and becomes about one date. What happens then is decided by three pieces of paper: the maturity and extension clauses, any take-out commitment, and the default and enforcement terms. Read them before you need them.

Recall

Q. What does an intercreditor agreement do?

A. It sets the rules between lenders at different levels of the stack: who is paid first, who may cure a default, and what each lender may and may not do when the borrower is in trouble.

Q. What is a stabilisation clause in a contract with a state?

A. A promise by the state that certain changes in law will not apply to the investor, or will be compensated, for a period. How far such a clause binds depends on the law and the treaty behind it.

Q. What is a trigger, in a stress-testing plan?

A. A pre-agreed measurable level, such as coverage falling below a stated number, at which a named person must take a named action.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, LEX here. Developers read the economic terms of a loan carefully and the maturity terms lightly, because maturity feels far away. But maturity is the one moment when the lender's position is strongest: the whole balance is due, and no cure period usually applies. The time to negotiate how that moment works is at signing, when you still have choices. This lesson teaches concepts. The details differ by jurisdiction and by document; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The maturity clause and the extension option

In plain English: the loan ends on a date, unless you meet stated conditions to make it end later.

The professional framing is the extension option: a contractual right to extend maturity, usually by six or twelve months at a time. Its value is in its conditions, which are commercial terms rather than legal standards. Typical conditions are: written notice within a window, often a set number of days before maturity; no default outstanding; payment of an extension fee; a coverage or debt yield test met at the time; sometimes a new appraisal showing loan to value below a stated level; and sometimes a rate cap extended or replaced. Each condition is a gate, and missing any one, including the notice window, can mean the option is lost.

A worked example, hypothetical. The loan says the borrower may extend once for six months on notice given not less than 60 and not more than 90 days before maturity, provided the debt yield is at least 9 percent. NOI is 1,600,000 dollars and the loan is 20,000,000 dollars, so debt yield, NOI divided by loan, is 8 percent. The option fails on its test. The borrower's real choices are to pay the loan down to about 17,780,000 dollars, the amount at which 1,600,000 is 9 percent, or to negotiate. Notice the asymmetry: the option exists when you do not need it and fails when you do. Negotiate the test at signing, so it is calibrated to the downside, not the base case.

The take-out commitment

In plain English: a permanent lender's promise to lend on completion is only as good as its conditions.

The professional framing is a forward or take-out commitment, sometimes combined with a tri-party or buy-sell agreement between the construction lender, the permanent lender and the borrower, under which the permanent lender agrees to buy or repay the construction loan when conditions are met. The conditions decide its worth: completion to approved plans, a minimum occupancy or rent level, a minimum coverage, no material adverse change, and a final date by which conditions must be met. A commitment with a short final date or a broad adverse-change clause may give little protection in exactly the market in which you need it.

Say that out loud now.

A commitment is only as good as its conditions and its final date.

Default at maturity

In plain English: if you do not repay on the date, the lender usually has its full rights at once.

The professional framing: failure to repay at maturity is usually an immediate event of default, without the grace and cure periods that may apply to a missed interest payment or a covenant breach. The lender may then charge default interest, a higher rate on the whole balance, call any guarantees and begin enforcement of its security. In practice, many lenders first agree a forbearance or standstill agreement: they promise not to enforce for a period in exchange for conditions, such as a paydown, fees, a sale process or new guarantees. Read those terms closely. A forbearance agreement often includes an acknowledgement that the default exists, a release of claims against the lender and a waiver of defences. You may be giving up more than you realise for a few months of time.

A second example, hypothetical. A lender offers 90 days of forbearance in exchange for a 1,000,000 dollar paydown, a 0.5 percent fee, appointment of a broker to sell, and a new guarantee of interest. The developer should ask four questions. What does the release give away? Does the new guarantee widen recourse beyond the original? What happens on day 91? And is the sale process controlled by the borrower or by the lender? A forbearance that turns a limited guarantee into a full one may cost more than the default.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach enforcing a mortgage after a maturity default. In Canada, enforcement procedure is provincial: some provinces rely mainly on a lender's power of sale, a contractual and statutory right to sell after notice, while others use court-supervised foreclosure or judicial sale, and notice periods and redemption rights differ by province. In Guyana, land and mortgage law reflect a mixed inheritance, and enforcement generally proceeds under its own statutes and court practice, with procedures and timelines that a lender will assess when pricing a loan [unverified — confirm independently]. The practical point for a developer in either place: the speed and certainty of enforcement shape how patient a lender can afford to be at maturity, and that shapes what you can negotiate. Verify against primary source before you rely on any of this.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, licensed where the property and the lender's security are located.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an extension option you think you have but cannot use, because its test was set to the base case or its notice window passed. The control is a covenant calendar: every notice window, test date and final date in the loan and any commitment, with a named owner and a reminder ninety days before each.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner signs a forbearance agreement as relief, without reading the release, the acknowledgement and the new guarantee. Relief bought with a wider guarantee is not relief.

Callback

In Week 39, LEX taught that a commitment letter binds only on its conditions, and that conditions precedent decide whether money moves. The same discipline applies at the other end of the loan. The extension option and the take-out commitment are conditions precedent to your exit; read them with the same suspicion you brought to the commitment letter.

Recap

An extension option is worth its conditions: notice, no default, a fee and a test, often set to the base case. A take-out commitment is worth its conditions and its final date. Default at maturity usually gives the lender immediate rights, and forbearance buys time at a price that can include a release and wider recourse. Keep a covenant calendar for every date.

Next: Nadia, on The Numbers: sizing the refinance at stabilisation, step by step.
checklist: I have read every condition of each extension option, including the notice window.
The extension tests are calibrated to my downside case, not my base case.
I know the conditions and final date of any take-out commitment.
I keep a covenant calendar with every notice and test date and a named owner.
I know what happens on default at maturity: default interest, guarantees and enforcement.
I will read any forbearance agreement's release, acknowledgement and new guarantees before signing.
I have a lawyer licensed where the property sits.
head: Field checklist
speak: At maturity, three pieces of paper decide what happens. First, the extension option: a right to extend on conditions, usually notice inside a window, no default, a fee and a coverage or debt yield test. Those tests are often set to the base case, so the option exists when I do not need it and fails when I do. I negotiate them to the downside at signing. Second, any take-out commitment: a permanent lender's promise to fund on completion, which is only as good as its conditions and final date. Third, default at maturity: usually an immediate event of default, with default interest, guarantees and enforcement available at once. Lenders often offer forbearance, but it can include a release of claims and a wider guarantee. I keep a covenant calendar of every date, and I verify every legal point with a lawyer licensed where the property sits.
terms: Debt yield — net operating income divided by the loan amount, a lender's measure of how much income supports each dollar lent.
Default interest — a higher rate charged on the whole balance once an event of default occurs.
Covenant calendar — a schedule of every notice window, test date and final date in the loan documents, with an owner and reminders.

hostile.q: Your extension needs a 9 percent debt yield and you are at 8. Why should I extend?
hostile.a: Because the shortfall is lease-up timing, not value, and I can show it. Here are the signed leases that take the debt yield above 9 percent within four months. I will pay down 1,000,000 dollars today, pay the fee, and accept a cash sweep until the test is met. I am not asking you to waive the test; I am asking for time to meet it, with my own money at risk first.

title: Sizing the Refinance at Stabilisation, Step by Step
summary: A worked calculation of a permanent loan at stabilisation, using value, coverage and debt yield tests, in a base case and a stressed case. The binding limit changes when the market moves, and the gap against the construction loan must be funded in the equity plan before the build starts.
body:
The refinance is sized by three tests at once, and the smallest answer wins. Run them at today's numbers and at stressed numbers, compare each with the construction loan balance, and you have the gap in dollars before it becomes a surprise.

Recall

Q. What does a stabilised building mean?

A. A building at its normal, sustainable level of occupancy and income, after lease-up, which is the state a permanent lender sizes its loan to.

Q. In the Week 43 currency stress, what was the break-even exchange rate?

A. The exchange rate at which the unhedged strategy's coverage fell to the covenant minimum: the point beyond which borrowing in a currency the project does not earn stops working.

Q. In Week 37, how were the layers of a stack built?

A. Band by band from the bottom of the value: senior debt to its loan-to-value and coverage limits, then mezzanine to a higher combined limit, then equity for the rest, each band tested on the downside.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Nadia here. Priya has shown what a late exit costs. Today we calculate the exit itself, line by line, with units at every step, so that you can do it on one page before you sign a construction loan and again every quarter after. All figures are hypothetical round numbers. Lending terms used here are commercial practice for illustration, not standards; real lenders set their own.

The facts

A finished 120-unit apartment building. Gross potential rent, the rent if every unit were let all year at asking rent, is 3,600,000 dollars a year. Vacancy and collection loss at stabilisation is 5 percent. Operating expenses are 1,320,000 dollars a year. The construction loan balance at completion, including capitalised interest, is 24,000,000 dollars. A permanent lender's indicative terms: maximum loan to value 65 percent; minimum debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), net operating income divided by annual debt service, of 1.25; minimum debt yield 8.5 percent; interest rate 6.5 percent; repayment over 30 years. The appraiser's exit cap rate is 6 percent.

Step 1: net operating income

Effective gross income is 3,600,000 dollars times 0.95, which is 3,420,000 dollars. Net operating income (NOI) is 3,420,000 less 1,320,000, which is 2,100,000 dollars a year. Every test below is built on this one number, so it must be stabilised income, not a hopeful annualised month.

Step 2: the value test

Value is NOI divided by the exit cap rate: 2,100,000 divided by 0.06 is 35,000,000 dollars. The loan-to-value limit allows 65 percent of that, which is 22,750,000 dollars.

Step 3: the coverage test

Maximum annual debt service is NOI divided by the minimum coverage: 2,100,000 divided by 1.25 is 1,680,000 dollars a year. To turn a payment into a loan, use the loan constant, the annual payment per dollar borrowed. For 6.5 percent over 30 years, paid monthly, the constant is about 7.58 percent. So the loan is 1,680,000 divided by 0.0758, about 22,150,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Income over coverage gives the payment; payment over the constant gives the loan.

Step 4: the debt yield test

The largest loan at an 8.5 percent debt yield is NOI divided by 0.085: 2,100,000 divided by 0.085 is about 24,710,000 dollars. Debt yield ignores interest rates and amortisation, which is why lenders like it: it cannot be flattered by a low rate.

Step 5: the binding limit and the gap

The three answers are 22,750,000 dollars by value, about 22,150,000 dollars by coverage and about 24,710,000 dollars by debt yield. The binding limit is the smallest: coverage, about 22,150,000 dollars. The construction loan balance is 24,000,000 dollars. The shortfall is about 1,850,000 dollars. Add closing costs, say 1 percent of the new loan, about 220,000 dollars. The cash needed at refinance is about 2,070,000 dollars, in the base case, with nothing having gone wrong.

Step 6: the stressed case

Now move the two numbers the market controls. The exit cap rate widens to 7 percent and the permanent rate rises to 7.5 percent. NOI is unchanged at 2,100,000 dollars, so this is a pure market move.

Value test: 2,100,000 divided by 0.07 is 30,000,000 dollars; 65 percent is 19,500,000 dollars. Coverage test: the payment limit is still 1,680,000 dollars; the constant at 7.5 percent over 30 years is about 8.39 percent, so the loan is 1,680,000 divided by 0.0839, about 20,020,000 dollars. Debt yield test: unchanged at about 24,710,000 dollars, because it does not see rates. The binding limit is now value, 19,500,000 dollars. The shortfall against 24,000,000 dollars is 4,500,000 dollars, plus about 195,000 dollars of costs: about 4,700,000 dollars.

Step 7: the table

TestBase caseStressed case
Value, 65 percent22,750,00019,500,000
Coverage, 1.25about 22,150,000about 20,020,000
Debt yield, 8.5 percentabout 24,710,000about 24,710,000
Binding loanabout 22,150,00019,500,000
Cash needed at refinanceabout 2,070,000about 4,700,000

All figures hypothetical, in dollars. Notice that the binding test changed from coverage to value when the market moved. Watch every test; the one that binds today may not bind at exit.

Step 8: what the numbers tell you to do

First, the base case already needs about 2,070,000 dollars. That money belongs in the equity plan on day one, not in a hope that rents will beat forecast. Second, the stressed case needs about 4,700,000 dollars. Either hold that as a reserve or committed equity, or reduce the construction loan so that the stressed take-out covers it. Third, ask what income would close the base gap. The refinance must repay 24,000,000 dollars plus about 240,000 dollars of costs, about 24,240,000 dollars. At the coverage test that needs annual debt service of 24,240,000 times 0.0758, about 1,837,000 dollars, and NOI of 1.25 times that, about 2,300,000 dollars, roughly 9.5 percent above plan. If your plan needs rents nearly 10 percent above the forecast to refinance, it is not a plan.

Step 9: check one answer forward

Always check backward work forward. A loan of 22,150,000 dollars at a constant of 7.58 percent costs about 1,679,000 dollars a year. NOI of 2,100,000 divided by 1,679,000 is about 1.25. The coverage test holds exactly at the limit, as it should.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is sizing the construction loan to the base-case take-out, so that any market move leaves a gap you must fund at the worst time. The control is to size the construction loan, or the reserve, to the stressed take-out, and to recompute all three tests every quarter.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner runs only the value test, because it is the one in the brochure, and misses that coverage binds first when rates are high. He also forgets closing costs, which are small and certain.

Callback

In Week 42, Priya reverse engineered a project loan from its coverage covenant: payment from income, loan from payment. Today you ran the same steps forward, and added the other two tests. The method is identical; only the lender changed. Learn one sizing routine and use it at every stage of the project's life.

Recap

Size the refinance by value, coverage and debt yield, and take the smallest. Compare it with the construction loan balance plus closing costs. Do it in the base case and in a stressed case with a wider cap rate and a higher rate. Fund the gap in the equity plan before you start.

Next: Priya, on The Room: the meeting with your construction lender when the take-out appraisal comes in low.
checklist: I calculate stabilised NOI from rent, vacancy and expenses, not from one good month.
I run the value, coverage and debt yield tests and take the smallest.
I use the loan constant to turn a payment limit into a loan amount.
I add closing costs to the amount the refinance must repay.
I rerun the tests at a wider cap rate and a higher interest rate.
I know which test binds today and which would bind in the stress.
I check every backward answer forward.
head: Field checklist
speak: The refinance is sized by three tests, and the smallest wins. Value: net operating income divided by the exit cap rate, times the loan-to-value limit. Coverage: income divided by the minimum coverage gives the maximum payment, and the payment divided by the loan constant gives the loan. Debt yield: income divided by the minimum debt yield. On hypothetical income of 2,100,000 dollars, a 6 percent cap rate and a 6.5 percent loan, coverage binds at about 22,150,000 dollars against a construction balance of 24,000,000, so I need about 2,070,000 dollars at refinance with nothing gone wrong. Stress the cap rate to 7 percent and the rate to 7.5, and value binds at 19,500,000 dollars: a gap of about 4,700,000. The binding test changed when the market moved. So I fund the gap in the equity plan before I start, and recompute all three tests every quarter.
terms: Loan constant — the annual debt payment per dollar borrowed, set by the interest rate and the repayment period.
Binding limit — the sizing test that produces the smallest loan, and therefore sets the loan.
Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) — net operating income divided by annual debt service.

hostile.q: Your take-out only works at a 6 percent cap rate. The last three sales in this market were at 6.75. Why is your number right?
hostile.a: It is not the number I rely on. At 7 percent the take-out is 19,500,000 dollars and the gap is about 4,700,000. My equity plan holds that amount as a committed reserve, so the refinance works at today's comparable sales and worse. If cap rates stay at 6.75, we release part of the reserve at refinance; if they widen, the reserve is already there.

title: The Meeting When the Take-Out Appraisal Comes In Low
summary: A low take-out appraisal ten months before maturity: how to meet the construction lender early, split the gap into time and value, commit your own money first and ask only for what time can fix. Includes the lines to say and never to say, two contrasting meetings, and the month's thread on decision journals.
body:
When the take-out appraisal comes in low, the meeting with your construction lender decides whether you are negotiating or being managed. Arrive early, with the number, the plan and your own money already committed.

Recall

Q. What is a forbearance agreement?

A. A lender's agreement, for a defined period and on conditions, not to enforce a default it is entitled to enforce. It often includes an acknowledgement of default and a release of claims.

Q. In a political-risk insurance underwriting call, what does the underwriter most want to know?

A. What exactly the investor wants covered, what has already been done to reduce the risk, and whether the investor will keep doing it, because insurance prices behaviour as well as country.

Q. How should you answer a mezzanine lender who asks why the senior loan is so large?

A. Show the senior loan sized to its tightest test on the downside, the cushion beneath the mezzanine, and the intercreditor rights that protect it, rather than arguing about the headline number.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Priya here. Every refinance plan meets reality at an appraisal. When the number is lower than the plan, you have a few months before maturity in which the lender still has choices and so do you. Wait until maturity and the lender's choices narrow to extend or enforce, and yours narrow to whatever it offers. The meeting I am about to describe is the most valuable meeting of the exit. All figures are hypothetical.

The scene

Month 26 of a 36-month construction loan of 24,000,000 dollars. The building is finished and 85 percent let. The permanent lender's appraisal has come in at a 6.75 percent cap rate instead of the 6 percent in your plan, so its loan offer is about 20,200,000 dollars. The gap at maturity, with costs, is about 4,000,000 dollars. You have asked for a meeting with the construction lender's relationship manager and its credit officer. The credit officer opens: "We saw the appraisal. What are you proposing?"

The question behind the question

The surface question is about your proposal. The real questions are two. Is this a timing problem or a value problem? And will this borrower put money in, or ask us to carry the risk? Everything you say should answer those two. If you open with the building's quality, you answer neither.

The lines to say

Open with the number, unsoftened. "The take-out is about 20,200,000 dollars against your 24,000,000. With costs, the gap is about 4,000,000. We are here ten months early because we want to close it with you, not at you."

Then the diagnosis. "Part of the gap is timing. At full stabilisation, about four months away, income rises enough to add roughly 1,000,000 dollars to the take-out. The rest, about 3,000,000, is the cap rate. That part time will not fix."

Then the plan, with your money first. "We propose three things. We pay down 1,500,000 dollars at maturity from committed equity. We bring in 1,500,000 dollars of preferred equity, with a term sheet in hand. And we ask for one six-month extension, with a cash sweep until the take-out closes, so the timing part can work."

Then the fallback. "If the permanent lender does not commit by month 32, we start a sale process and keep you informed weekly."

Say that out loud now.

Here is the gap, here is how much is time and how much is value, here is my money, here is the fallback.

The lines never to say

Never say "the appraiser got it wrong" unless you can show comparable sales that prove it; it sounds like denial. Never say "we just need a bit more time" when part of the gap is value. Never say "you would not want to take the building back"; the lender knows its options, and a threat invites it to prove it is not afraid. Never promise a take-out date you do not control.

When to stay silent

After you state your paydown, stop. The credit officer is now calculating its own exposure with your money in it. If you keep talking, you start negotiating against yourself, offering more before anyone has asked. Let the lender ask its next question; the question tells you what it still needs.

Holding your state

A low appraisal feels like a verdict on your judgment, and that feeling makes people talk fast and defend. Before the meeting, write the gap and the three-part plan on one card and read it aloud twice. In the meeting, slow your speech and keep your hands still. Kema's rule from Week 4: the outbreath longer than the inbreath, before you answer the hardest question.

Worked examples: two meetings

Meeting one. The developer waits until month 35. He arrives without a plan and asks for a twelve-month extension. The lender, now at maturity, offers 90 days of forbearance with a new full-recourse guarantee, default interest and a lender-controlled sale. The developer signs because the alternative is enforcement. The gap of 4,000,000 dollars has become a personal guarantee of 24,000,000.

Meeting two. The developer meets at month 26, separates time from value, commits 1,500,000 dollars and a term sheet for 1,500,000 more, and asks for six months with a sweep. The lender agrees, adding a condition that the preferred equity close within sixty days. The developer loses some profit to the preferred equity and keeps the building.

After the meeting

Within a day, send a one-page note: the appraisal, the gap split into time and value, the three commitments with dates, the fallback trigger and who owns each action. Ask the lender to confirm its conditions in writing. Then diarise every date on your covenant calendar.

Monthly thread: decision journals

Before this meeting, write a short entry in your decision journal: what you expect the lender to say, what you will accept, and what would make you start a sale instead. Write it before, not after, because memory rewrites itself to look wise.

Afterwards, add what happened and one sentence on what you got wrong. Over many exits, that journal becomes your own reference class: how often appraisals came in low, by how much and how lenders responded. That is better evidence than any broker's opinion.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is arriving late, so that the lender's choices have narrowed to the ones that cost you most. The control is a refinance start date twelve months before maturity and a rule that a low appraisal triggers a lender meeting within two weeks.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the lender as an obstacle to be persuaded rather than a counterparty with its own problem to solve. Solve the lender's problem, its exposure and its confidence in you, and the extension usually follows.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the hostile question: acknowledge, bridge, answer. The credit officer's opening is exactly that kind of question. Acknowledge the appraisal, bridge to the diagnosis, answer with the plan. The structure keeps you from defending the past when the room wants the future.

Recap

Meet early. State the gap plainly, split it into time and value, commit your own money first, ask for only what time will fix, and give a fallback with a date. Stay silent after the paydown. Write it up within a day.

Next: Kema, with the week's review: six questions, the Red Pen and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I meet the lender within two weeks of a low appraisal, not at maturity.
I state the gap in dollars, with costs, in the first sentence.
I split the gap into the part time will fix and the part it will not.
I commit my own money before I ask for anything.
I offer a fallback with a trigger date.
I stay silent after stating my paydown.
I send a one-page note within a day and ask for the lender's conditions in writing.
I write a decision journal entry before the meeting.
head: Field checklist
speak: When the take-out appraisal comes in low, I meet the construction lender early, ten months before maturity rather than at it, while both of us still have choices. I open with the number: the take-out, the balance and the gap with costs. Then the diagnosis: how much of the gap is timing, which more income will fix, and how much is value, which time will not fix. Then my money first: a paydown from committed equity and a term sheet for new equity. Then I ask only for what time can fix, say a six-month extension with a cash sweep. Then a fallback: a sale process if the permanent lender has not committed by a stated date. After the paydown, I stop talking. I never blame the appraiser without evidence, never threaten, and never promise a date I do not control. Within a day, I send one page and ask for the lender's conditions in writing.
terms: Cash sweep — a loan term under which surplus cash goes to repay the loan rather than to the borrower, until a stated condition is met.
Preferred equity — equity that ranks ahead of common equity for its return, but behind all debt.
Reference class — a set of similar past cases used to estimate how often, and by how much, an outcome happens.

hostile.q: You missed your appraisal by three quarters of a point. Why should I believe your next number?
hostile.a: You should not rely on my number; rely on the plan that works at the appraiser's. At 6.75 percent the gap is about 4,000,000 dollars. I am paying down 1,500,000 from committed equity, I have a term sheet for 1,500,000 of preferred equity, and the rest closes with four months of income growth already signed in leases. If the take-out is not committed by month 32, I start a sale, and you will hear it from me first.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 45 Review: Exit Financing, Take-Outs and the Maturity Gap
summary: Six questions with answers on take-out financing, exit cap rates, maturity gaps, bridge loans, extension options and refinance sizing. A recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a flawed refinance memo, and a two-minute boardroom drill with a model answer.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: the construction loan is repaid by an exit you do not yet have, so size that exit at stressed numbers, reach it before maturity, and fund the gap before you start.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause in the take-out composite?

A. A construction loan term shorter than the project's own realistic path to a refinance, combined with an exit sized at the going-in cap rate. The building was financed; the exit was assumed.

Q. What did Week 43 teach about borrowing in a foreign currency?

A. Never borrow in a currency the project does not earn unless the mismatch is hedged or reserved against and sized to survive a severe devaluation.

Q. What is the difference between senior and mezzanine debt in a default?

A. Senior debt is repaid first from the asset; mezzanine is repaid only after senior, and its remedies are limited by the intercreditor agreement, so it absorbs losses first.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Kema here. Exit financing is where everything you learned in this phase gets tested on one date. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is take-out financing, and why is it a risk on the day you sign the construction loan?

Answer: It is the permanent loan or sale that repays the construction loan once the building earns. It is a risk because you do not have it yet: it will be sized to value and income at the time of refinance, in a market you do not control.

Question 2. Why is the exit cap rate described as the size of your next loan?

Answer: Because value is income divided by the cap rate, and the permanent lender's loan-to-value test is a percentage of that value. On 2,000,000 dollars of income, 6 percent gives about 33,330,000 dollars and 7 percent about 28,570,000, so at 65 percent the loan falls by about 3,100,000 dollars.

Question 3. What is a maturity gap, and what are the three ways to close it?

Answer: The time between the loan's due date and the earliest realistic take-out. You close it with an extension option, a bridge loan or a sale, and each has a cost and conditions.

Question 4. When is a bridge loan the right tool?

Answer: When the cause of the gap is time: a building that will support its permanent loan once stabilised. When the cause is value, a bridge only moves the gap to a more expensive lender.

Question 5. Why might an extension option fail when you need it?

Answer: Because its conditions, such as a debt yield or coverage test, are often set to the base case, and a missed notice window can lose it. Negotiate the tests to the downside at signing and keep a covenant calendar.

Question 6. How do you size a refinance?

Answer: By value, coverage and debt yield, taking the smallest, then compare with the construction balance plus closing costs. Do it in the base case and in a stressed case with a wider cap rate and higher rate.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Nadia framed the exit as a second loan you do not yet have, and measured the maturity gap. Ford and Roman took a composite case in which a well-built building was lost to its maturity date, giving Rule 45. Priya priced the four costs of a late exit. LEX read the extension option, the take-out commitment and default at maturity, and compared mortgage enforcement in Canada and Guyana. Nadia sized a refinance by three tests. Priya ran the meeting when the appraisal came in low.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical refinance memo and find the defects before reading on.

Refinance memo, Project Alpha. The building will stabilise in month 34. The construction loan matures in month 30, with one six-month extension available at our option. Stabilised NOI is 2,100,000 dollars, based on the strong lease-up in month 29 annualised. At the going-in cap rate of 6 percent, value is 35,000,000 dollars, and at 65 percent the take-out is 22,750,000 dollars, which repays the construction loan of 22,500,000 dollars. No equity is required at refinance. A bridge is available as a fallback if needed.

The defects. First, the loan matures four months before stabilisation, and the memo treats the extension as certain ("at our option") without stating its conditions or testing them. Second, the NOI is one strong month annualised, not stabilised income. Third, the exit uses the going-in cap rate with no stressed case. Fourth, only the value test is run; coverage and debt yield, either of which may bind, are missing. Fifth, closing costs and capitalised interest during the extension are ignored, so the 250,000 dollar margin is likely negative. Sixth, "a bridge is available" is not a plan: no lender, price, or proof that the stabilised building repays it.

Corrected, the memo would state the extension conditions and the date they will be tested, use stabilised NOI, run all three tests at the going-in rate and one point worse, include costs, and name the funded source for the stressed gap.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "How do we actually pay off the construction loan?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "The construction loan is repaid by an exit we do not have yet, a permanent loan or a sale. The permanent lender sizes its loan to the finished, stabilised building by three tests, value, coverage and debt yield, and lends the smallest. Value depends on the exit cap rate, so a one-point move can cut the loan by millions. So we do three things. We size the take-out at a cap rate a point above today's and at a higher rate, and put the gap in the equity plan now. We make sure the loan's term, with extensions, reaches past our realistic stabilisation date, and we negotiate the extension tests to the downside. And we start the refinance a year before maturity, so if the appraisal is low we meet the lender with a plan while both sides still have choices. A bridge loan is our tool only if the gap is time, not value."

Score your own answer. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name the three tests? Did you say why the exit cap rate matters? Did you name a date to start the refinance? Did you finish inside two minutes? Record it again tomorrow if not.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is treating the exit as the end of the project's story instead of its hardest financing. The control is the exit card: maturity, stabilisation, three tests at stressed numbers, the gap and its funded source, updated every quarter.

The beginner's mistake

Learning the vocabulary, take-out, bridge, extension, and never running the three tests on his own pro forma. Run them this week.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught the in-balance test: the money left must cover the cost to complete. The exit is the same test on the last day: the take-out must cover the balance plus costs. If it does not, the project is out of balance at maturity, and someone with equity or a guarantee closes the gap.

Recap

The exit is a second financing. Size it by three tests at stressed numbers, close the maturity gap in advance, use a bridge only for time, read every extension condition, and meet the lender early when the appraisal is low. Rule 45 holds it together.

head: The six questions
speak: This week came down to one sentence: the construction loan is repaid by an exit I do not yet have. The permanent lender sizes to the stabilised building by value, coverage and debt yield, and lends the smallest. Value depends on the exit cap rate, so I size the take-out at a cap rate a point above today's and at a higher interest rate, and I put the gap in the equity plan before I start. I make sure the loan's term with extensions reaches past my realistic stabilisation date, and I negotiate extension tests to the downside. I start the refinance a year before maturity. If the appraisal comes in low, I meet the lender early, split the gap into time and value, put my money in first and ask only for what time can fix. A bridge loan is for time, never for value. Rule 45: never let a construction loan mature before the building can carry its own refinance at a stressed exit cap rate.
terms: Exit card — a one-page record of maturity, stabilisation, the three refinance tests at stressed numbers, the gap and its funded source.
Stressed take-out — the permanent loan sized at a wider cap rate and higher interest rate than today's.
Refinance gap — the cash needed when the take-out loan is smaller than the construction balance plus costs.

hostile.q: Your refinance memo says no equity is needed. Show me why I should believe that.
hostile.a: You should not, until you see three tests rather than one. On stabilised income, not a strong month annualised, the value, coverage and debt yield tests give the take-out, and at a cap rate one point above going-in the gap is shown in dollars, with closing costs and extension interest. The equity plan funds that gap, and the extension conditions are tested on a stated date, so the memo no longer depends on the going-in cap rate holding.
